# `extern "C"`

There is exactly one way to reach outside the language: declare a C function in
an `extern "C"` block. No bodies, no generics, no variadic parameters — a
declaration, and a promise that the symbol is there at link time.

## The shape

```tripon
use tier core;

extern "C" {
    fn puts(s: str) -> i32;
    fn putchar(c: i32) -> i32;
}
```

The block is top-level, next to `fn`, `struct` and `enum`. It may appear more
than once, and the order relative to the call does not matter: declarations are
collected before any body is checked. The name in the declaration is the C
symbol name; there is no rename and no link-name attribute.

Each entry takes the same parameter and return syntax as a Tripon function. A
return type of `()` maps to C `void`. Calling one is an ordinary call:

```tripon
use tier core;

extern "C" {
    fn puts(s: str) -> i32;
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    let wrote = puts("via extern");
    print_i32(wrote);
    return 0;
}
```

<Session lines={["via extern", "11", ""]} />

`puts` printed the string and then returned 11 — the ten characters plus the
newline it appended. The empty line is that newline arriving before `print_i32`
wrote `11`. An extern call's return value is a normal Tripon value; you can bind
it, compare it, or drop it.

## The type mapping

The declaration is emitted as a C prototype with these types:

| Tripon | C |
|---|---|
| `i8` `i16` `i32` `i64` | `int8_t` `int16_t` `int32_t` `int64_t` |
| `u8` `u16` `u32` `u64` | `uint8_t` `uint16_t` `uint32_t` `uint64_t` |
| `isize` `usize` | `intptr_t` `uintptr_t` |
| `f32` `f64` | `float` `double` |
| `bool` | `bool` |
| `str` | `const char *` |
| `()` | `void` |
| struct, enum | its `tp_`-prefixed typedef |

The block above emits:

```c
/* ---- extern blocks ---- */
extern int32_t puts(const char *);
extern int32_t putchar(int32_t);
```

That is the whole bridge. A `str` is passed as `const char *`; no length is
carried, because Tripon's `str` does not carry one either.

## The prototype must match the real one

The generated C includes the platform headers — `stdio.h`, `stdlib.h`,
`string.h`, `math.h` — before the extern block. If your declaration disagrees
with the header's prototype, the C compiler sees two declarations of one symbol
and refuses:

<Session
  lines={[
    "$ ralt build printf.tp",
    "build/printf.c:48:16: error: conflicting types for ‘printf’; have ‘int32_t(const char *)’ {aka ‘int(const char *)’}",
    "   48 | extern int32_t printf(const char *);",
    "      |                ^~~~~~",
    "In file included from build/printf.c:4:",
    "/usr/include/stdio.h:370:12: note: previous declaration of ‘printf’ with type ‘int(const char *, ...)’",
  ]}
/>

`printf` is variadic, and Tripon has no `...` in a parameter list, so there is
no correct declaration to write. Use `puts` or `putchar` for output, or declare a
non-variadic wrapper that your C side provides.

The same thing happens when the types are merely wider or unsigned:
`fn srand(seed: i32) -> ()` conflicts with the header's `void srand(unsigned
int)`. The fix is to match the real signature, or leave the function alone.

Functions with non-variadic prototypes that already match work without
ceremony:

```tripon
use tier core;

extern "C" {
    fn fabs(x: f64) -> f64;
    fn fmod(x: f64, y: f64) -> f64;
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    print_f64(fabs(-2.5));
    print_f64(fmod(7.0, 2.0));
    return 0;
}
```

<Session lines={["2.50", "1.00"]} />

Both symbols come from the C library the build already links. There is no flag
in v0 for adding a library or an object file to the link; if the symbol is not
in the default link, the call fails at `cc` and that is the end of it.

## Tier

`extern` is available at `kernel`, not just `core`. A kernel-tier file that
declares `puts` and calls it builds:

<Session
  lines={[
    "$ ralt run kernel_extern.tp",
    "kernel extern",
  ]}
/>

That is deliberate: the lowest tier is exactly where a program needs to talk to
the platform. What the tier buys is that nothing *else* is available.

## What this costs

Everything else in Tripon is built to keep a promise: no undefined behaviour, a
defined trap for the four arithmetic edges, a span for every diagnostic. An
`extern` call is where that promise stops. The compiler checks the arguments
against the declaration, and then the call is a C call:

- the C function may read past a string you passed;
- it may return a value that is not in the range you expect;
- it may not return at all.

The declaration cannot be verified, only declared. Treat an `extern` block as
an audit point: each one is a function whose behaviour is outside the language,
and the review question is whether you trust it. The [no-UB
page](/docs/language/traps) covers what is guaranteed everywhere else.

## What is refused at check time

| written | result |
|---|---|
| call to a name with no declaration | E0201 `call to unknown function 'puts'` |
| wrong argument count | E0202 `'puts' takes 1 argument(s), got 0` |
| wrong argument type | E0202, naming both types |
| an extern declaration with a body | parse error |
| variadic `...` | parse error |

The first row is the one that surprises C programmers: there is no implicit
libc prelude. A `.tp` file that calls `puts` without the block is not linked
against libc by accident; it is E0201 at check time. Importing a symbol is a line
of source, and that is the point.
